title: The Monty Hall Problem: Why Intuition Fails at Probability
question: Why does almost everyone, including trained mathematicians, get a simple three-door puzzle wrong?
summary: Switching doors in the Monty Hall game wins two-thirds of the time. The puzzle is less about arithmetic than about how information, and the process that generates it, changes what we should believe.
content:
The game

You face three doors: a car behind one, goats behind two. You pick a door. The host, who knows where the car is, opens a different door revealing a goat, then offers you the chance to switch. Should you?

The answer that offends intuition

Yes. Switching wins with probability 2/3; staying wins with 1/3. When Marilyn vos Savant published this in 1990, thousands of readers, including professors, wrote to insist she was wrong. Paul Erdős reportedly refused to accept it until shown a computer simulation.

Why it works

Your first pick is right 1/3 of the time. That doesn't change when the host opens a door, because the host never reveals the car and never opens your door. The remaining 2/3 of probability, which sat on the two doors you didn't choose, collapses onto the single unopened one. Imagine a hundred doors: you pick one, the host opens ninety-eight goat doors. Switching now obviously concentrates the odds.

The hidden assumption

The result depends on the host's rules. If the host opens a random door and merely happens to reveal a goat, switching and staying are equal at 1/2. The same observation carries different evidential weight depending on the process behind it. This is Bayes' theorem in disguise: what you learn depends on how likely each hypothesis was to produce what you saw.

Why our minds balk

People reason 'two doors left, so fifty-fifty', treating the situation as a fresh, symmetric choice. We neglect the history that made the doors unequal. Studies suggest even pigeons learn to switch faster than humans, since they follow frequencies rather than a flawed mental model. There is also an emotional asymmetry: regret from switching away from a winner feels worse than regret from staying with a loser.

A lesson beyond games

Medical tests, legal evidence, and news all arrive through filtering processes. A positive result means little without knowing base rates and how the test behaves. Monty Hall is a clean laboratory for a messy truth: information is never separate from its source.

perspectives.title: Bayesian statistics
perspectives.description: Updating on the host's action requires modelling why the host acted. Under the standard rules, the evidence shifts probability to the unchosen door.

perspectives.title: Cognitive psychology
perspectives.description: Humans substitute a simple symmetric frame ('two options, equal odds') for the real conditional structure, showing how heuristics misfire on counterintuitive structure.

perspectives.title: Game theory
perspectives.description: The host is a constrained player whose strategy defines the information content of the reveal. Changing the host's policy changes the optimal response.

perspectives.title: Education
perspectives.description: Simulation, extreme cases like 100 doors, and frequency framing turn an offensive answer into an obvious one, a model for teaching probability.

connections: Bayes' theorem and the base rate fallacy
openQuestions: Why does a correct formal argument often fail to change intuition until we see simulations?
How should we reason when we don't know the process that generates our evidence?
Is there a framing of probability that matches human intuition rather than fighting it?
How much of everyday misjudgement of risk stems from ignoring selection effects?
